quote: Oh my goodness. You're paying 429 a month?
stewart_read: This is the genuine bill-anchor moment in the call — spontaneous, emotionally real reaction. It briefly builds trust but is never followed with a flip tying the number to urgency or to what the appointment would show the customer.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to follow a strong reaction like this with a forward pull, e.g. tying the $429 to what a design review would show, instead of letting the moment pass into the next verify question.

quote: The only thing that you need to qualify for those programs is that you have a credit score above 670.
stewart_read: The rep states the 670 threshold correctly per script, and the schema itself flags this as an open policy question (stated credit vs. pulled credit) rather than a rep error. This is not a protocol violation — the rep followed procedure as documented.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as an error (protocol_violation) but the schema explicitly notes the threshold and stated-vs-pulled ambiguity is a live Kenny policy question, not something the rep got wrong.
coaching_implication: Flag for the manager as a floor-wide policy question, not an individual coaching gap: is the setter supposed to DQ on stated credit, or should stated-sub-670 customers still be passed to the closer for an actual pull? Until Kenny resolves this, the rep followed the documented rule correctly.

quote: I've seen I've been seeing that the government is helping out with, with the solar. I don't know.
stewart_read: The customer names a real interest driver (government incentives). The rep does briefly reference state incentives right after this ('we have lots of in like, state incentives...that will help pay for your guys' system'), so the reason wasn't ignored outright, but the acknowledgment is generic and immediately pivots into the credit qualifier rather than being sustained or tied back to the bill pain just established.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep could be read as having used the reason since incentives are mentioned in the same breath, but the reference is a single sentence with no follow-up or reinforcement later in the call.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to hold the incentive-interest thread a beat longer — connect it explicitly to the $429 bill just anchored — before moving into qualification, so the customer feels the motivator was heard, not just checked off.

quote: So if I were you, I would just give us a callback when your guys' credit is high enough, and then we would be able to get you all of those incentives.
stewart_read: This is a soft exit with no owned next step — the rep tells the customer to call back rather than setting any kind of callback date or check-in the rep owns. This is a reactive close, not a strategic deferral; there's no mechanism to re-engage this lead.
alternative_hypothesis: A strategic read would be that the credit gate is a hard DQ and no further action is warranted, but even a hard DQ call can end with the rep offering to follow up in a set timeframe rather than putting the burden entirely on the customer.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to own the next touch even on a DQ — e.g., a note to check back in a set number of months — rather than leaving re-engagement entirely to the customer's initiative.

quote: We had good credit and then and then something went wrong. And I think he's only it's 630.
stewart_read: The customer discloses what sounds like a financial hardship ('something went wrong') affecting their credit. The rep does not acknowledge this at all — no empathetic beat, straight into 'Do you know what yours is sitting at.'
coaching_implication: This is a trust-gift disclosure per the schema's vulnerability framework. Coach the rep to pause and acknowledge before moving to the next verify question — even a brief 'that happens to a lot of folks' keeps the human connection alive before the DQ lands.

quote: Okay. And what was your name? I don't think I ever asked.
stewart_read: The rep is over a minute into a live conversation with this customer — having already discussed her bill and address — before asking her name. It's caught and repaired here, but it's a rapport gap that made the early part of the call feel transactional.
coaching_implication: Small process fix: get the caller's name in the first 15-20 seconds, before diving into bill and address questions, so the conversation feels personal from the start.

quote: Yes. I've seen I've been seeing that the government is helping out with, with the solar. I don't know.
stewart_read: Customer proactively raises awareness of solar incentives unprompted — a genuine interest signal, not just a bill-pain response. This shows some independent research/motivation beyond just being called.
coaching_implication: Manager should note this as a positive lead-quality signal the rep could have leaned into harder — a customer who's already looked into incentives is more sales-ready than a cold contact, and that warrants more effort before a DQ closes the door.

quote: So is that the case for you or for your husband?
stewart_read: The rep correctly includes both Leroy and Armadina in the credit question rather than assuming only the primary contact matters, which aligns with treating both title-holders as co-decision-makers.
coaching_implication: This is a small positive — worth noting to the rep that checking both parties' credit status is the right instinct, distinct from the DQ decision itself which is a separate policy question.
